fields.meta_description: Build expense report automation that turns receipts into report lines, holds out-of-policy spend for a note, and routes each approval. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build Expense Report Automation That Follows Your Policy
fields.hero_description: Build expense report automation that turns receipt photos into report lines and sends each report to the right approver.
fields.features_heading: What Runs Between the Receipt and the Approval
fields.features_subheading: Each report is checked against your policy before an approver opens it. Emergent builds the whole flow from a plain-English prompt.
fields.feature_1:
Receipt photos turn into report lines

The app reads the merchant and total from a photo or an emailed PDF and adds the line to the open report, dated and categorized. A faded total waits for the employee to confirm.
fields.feature_2:
Your policy, written as rules

Type the limits as your handbook states them: a nightly hotel cap, a meal limit per person, receipts above an amount you pick. A line that breaks one asks for a reason.
fields.feature_3:
Approvers chosen by amount and team

Small reports stop at the employee's manager, larger ones add finance, and a department head can join for their team's spend. Describe a new order to change the chain.
fields.feature_4:
Decisions from Slack or email

Approvers see the total, the flagged lines, and the receipts in a Slack or email message and decide there. A report left waiting sends a reminder, then escalates to a backup.
fields.feature_5:
Connected to the systems you already run

The app reads your employee and manager list from the HR system and posts approved reports to QuickBooks, Xero, or NetSuite. Any other tool with an API connects too.
fields.feature_6:
Records you keep, approvers you add freely

Every report and its approvals live in a database you own. There are no per-approver seats to count, and paid plans export the full code to your GitHub repository on request.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Stops Between Receipt and Approval
fields.tab_content_1:
Every Denver receipt lands on one trip report

Tamsin Achebe photographs 4 receipts on a client trip to Denver. The app reads each one into a line on her trip report: a $318.00 flight, $412.00 for 2 hotel nights, a $46.80 lunch, and a $27.20 taxi. The report totals $804.00 and is ready to submit.
fields.tab_content_2:
Dinners over $75 a head need a note first

Tallowmere Consulting allows $75 per person for a client dinner. Gideon Farrow adds a $212.40 dinner for 2, which comes to $106.20 a head, so the app flags the line before he submits. His report waits until he writes a note on why the dinner ran over.
fields.tab_content_3:
Reports over $1,000 go on to finance

Ingrid Halvorsen submits a $1,640.00 conference report, and her manager, Rufus Adeyemi, approves it from a Slack message. Because the total is over $1,000, the report then goes to finance lead Marguerite Sato in a Slack message of her own. An approver who has not answered in 2 days gets a reminder.
fields.tab_content_4:
QuickBooks gets each report, finance gets the totals

Every approved report syncs to QuickBooks as one entry, coded by the categories on its lines. Marguerite sees October's $14,260 of approved spend by department on a dashboard: Field Research at $8,420, Sales at $4,180, and Operations at $1,660.

fields.howto_description: These 7 steps get expense report automation checking each line against your policy and sending each report to its approver.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the policy the way employees already follow it: the meal limit per person, the hotel cap per night, the amount above which a receipt is required, and who approves what. Keep every number exact, because each one becomes a rule.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Tell Emergent in plain English how a report travels: an employee adds receipts, each line is checked, and the report goes to the manager, then to finance above your threshold. Emergent builds the app and its approval screens from that prompt.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Connect the accounting software and the HR system. The app reads your expense categories from the ledger, and it takes each employee's approver from the reporting lines in HR.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick Slack, email, or the app's own approval screen for each approver. Set how long a report can wait before a reminder goes out, and name the backup who gets it after that.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Run last month's reports through the app before anyone files a new one. Compare its flags with what finance caught by hand, and adjust a rule wherever the two disagree.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the app to the team that travels the most and let them file real trips for a month. If a rule flags nearly every report, it is set too tight: loosen it before the next team joins.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Add the next rule set once the first runs cleanly: mileage, a daily meal allowance, or a separate chain for one department. Each change is a new prompt to Emergent.

faq_plan.a: Expense report automation is software that checks and routes expense reports by rule. An expense report is a categorized and itemized list of expenses that were made on behalf of the organization. The automation reads each receipt into that list, tests every line against company policy, and sends the finished report to its approvers.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up expense report automation?
faq_plan.a: Start with your written expense policy and one report flow. Describe the limits, the receipt rules, and who approves what to Emergent's AI automation builder, and it builds the report screens, the policy checks, and the approval chain. When the policy changes, you update the app by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: Who should approve each step in an expense approval workflow?
faq_plan.a: Put the employee's manager first, because the manager knows whether the trip or purchase was needed. Add finance above an amount you choose to check coding and policy, and add a department head only for spend against their own budget. Name a backup for each approver, and a report keeps moving while someone is out.

faq_plan.q: Can expense report automation show spending by department?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Each approved report carries the employee's department, and the app can total approved spend per department, per month, on a dashboard for the finance lead. For monthly finance packs that pull numbers from several systems, see report automation.

faq_plan.q: How does expense report automation handle a missing receipt?
faq_plan.a: It holds the line until the employee attaches a receipt or fills in a missing-receipt note: what was bought, where, when, and for what business purpose. Your policy decides whether a note is enough, and above what amount an approver has to read it before signing off.

faq_plan.q: Can expense report automation catch duplicate expenses?
faq_plan.a: It can flag them for a person to decide. Add a rule that compares each new line's amount and date with lines already filed, and a match reaches the approver marked as a possible duplicate. The app Emergent builds keeps the flagged lines and each decision in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How does expense report automation post approved reports to the accounting software?
faq_plan.a: Through the accounting software's API. When the last approver signs off, the app posts the report to QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, or another ledger with an API. Decide before you connect whether a report posts as one entry or as one entry per line. For bank matching and the rest of the close, see accounting automation.

faq_plan.q: Can employees use expense report automation from their phones?
faq_plan.a: Yes. An employee photographs the receipt on a phone. The app then asks what it needs one question per screen, such as how many people were at a dinner or which client the trip was for. The report fills in as the answers arrive.

faq_plan.q: Which policy rules can expense report automation check?
faq_plan.a: Any rule you can state with a number, a date, or a list. Examples include an approved hotel list, a total per trip, a filing deadline after the trip ends, or a ban on alcohol lines. Rules that need judgment, such as whether a dinner was for a client, stay with the approver. Emergent writes each rule from your description, and you change one by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: Does expense report automation remove the need to type in receipt details?
faq_plan.a: For receipts the app can read, yes. Typing is left for what a receipt does not show: the business purpose and, for a meal, who attended. For other paperwork that still gets retyped, such as supplier forms or field sheets, see data entry automation.

plan.angle: The top 10 are expense software vendors (Concur, Ramp, Fyle, Brex, Navan) and finance explainers (NetSuite, Wise, Amex, Planergy) that describe automated expense reporting in general terms and sell their own tool. None shows one report moving through the steps with real amounts. This page follows one consulting firm's October: receipts from one trip turned into report lines, a dinner over the firm's own per-person limit held for a note, a $1,640.00 report routed past $1,000 to finance, and approved reports synced to the accounting software with spend by department. Every limit is the company's own policy, never tax advice, and the page stays on employee-paid expenses, leaving vendor bills to the accounts payable and invoice pages.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build Expense Report Automation That Follows Your Policy'; hero 'Build expense report automation that turns receipt photos into report lines and sends each report to the right approver.' covers capture, policy and approval, not one feature; how-to description one sentence under 140 chars.

intent.evidence: Top 10 are expense vendors and explainers; page defines the term in FAQ 1 (Zoho-sourced), shows one report moving receipt -> policy -> approval -> QuickBooks with real amounts, and gives a 7-step how-to ('01 Write down your policy' ... '07 Add the next rule set').

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: 'a nightly hotel cap, a meal limit per person', 'Reports over $1,000 go on to finance', 'missing-receipt note: what was bought, where, when, and for what business purpose'. Table from library (automation set).

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: 'Tamsin Achebe photographs 4 receipts...', 'Tallowmere Consulting allows $75 per person...', 'Every approved report syncs to QuickBooks...'; feature bodies open on verbs or subjects ('The app reads...', 'Type the limits...').

craft.evidence: Sentences carry one idea each; one ', so' ending in tab_content_2 ('...$106.20 a head, so the app flags the line') under the Q5 limit; no blocking craft defects.

voice.evidence: Calm, product-led copy: 'A faded total waits for the employee to confirm.' 'If a rule flags nearly every report, it is set too tight: loosen it before the next team joins.' No AI tells; one wording note on feature 6.

truth.evidence: Numbers agree: 318.00+412.00+46.80+27.20 = $804.00; $212.40/2 = $106.20 > $75; 8,420+4,180+1,660 = $14,260. Definition matches the Zoho quote ('categorized and itemized list of expenses that were made on behalf of the organization'). Emergent claims map to prompt-build, ai-extraction, alerts, api-connect, database-owned, no-caps, code-export, conversational, free-start. No tax or financial advice: every limit is 'the company's own policy'.

distinct.evidence: Stays on employee-paid spend (trip receipts, dinners, conference reports); no vendor bills, POs or invoice matching, so no overlap with accounts-payable-automation or invoice-automation; sibling primaries appear only as FAQ link anchors (report automation, accounting automation, data entry automation).

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions, none branded or format asks (paa --spec: pass 10, reject 0); each answered in the first sentence ('It can flag them for a person to decide.', 'Through the accounting software's API.'); hub link in item 2; secondary 'expense approval workflow' in item 3.
